Exposition

Do Gaussian Spaces Remain Different in Infinite Dimensions After Forgetting Sign or Phase?

Source paper
This explanation is based on the public version arXiv:2609.07030v2

This page is an explanation, not the original paper.

This page explains "Hopf quotients of the infinite-dimensional Gaussian pyramid" (arXiv:2609.07030v2, September 24, 2026), a paper I wrote jointly with my advisor Takashi Shioya [15]. It treats the pyramid Γ∞\Gamma^\inftyΓ∞ of infinite-dimensional Gaussian space and its two quotients, Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/Z2​ (forget the overall sign) and Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/U(1) (forget the common phase), and shows that no two of them coincide after any rescaling of distance (Theorem A), together with the proof. Numbers of theorems, lemmas and equations follow this fixed public version v2.

The prerequisites are calculus, linear algebra, the expectation and variance of random variables, and some experience reading proofs. Metric measure spaces, pyramids and Wiener chaos are introduced only as far as they are used. Theorems that the paper quotes as known results (the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality, completeness of the Hermite decomposition, hypercontractivity) are stated in usable form and their proofs are omitted; the places where they enter are marked in the text and in the table at the end.

Theorems and lemmas set in a quotation block are claims of the paper. Paragraphs beginning "Explainer's note.", together with the figure, the numerical examples and the checks, are additions of mine for readability and are not statements of the paper. Where the source's wording needed a repair, the passage is marked "Distinction from the source."

Question | Do the sign-forgetting limit and the phase-forgetting limit stay different when the unit of distance is changed?

The sphere Sn(n)S^n(\sqrt n)Sn(n​) of large dimension nnn approaches the infinite-dimensional standard Gaussian space (below, the Gaussian pyramid) Γ∞\Gamma^\inftyΓ∞. The quotient Sn(n)/Z2S^n(\sqrt n)/\mathbb Z_2Sn(n​)/Z2​, which corresponds to real projective space, and the quotient S2n+1(2n+1)/U(1)S^{2n+1}(\sqrt{2n+1})/U(1)S2n+1(2n+1​)/U(1), which corresponds to complex projective space, approach Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/Z2​ and Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/U(1) respectively. These convergences were proved by Shioya [15, 16] and extended to the canonical Riemannian metrics by Kazukawa [11] (as stated in the introduction). A convergence theorem says what the limit is; it does not say whether the three limits differ from one another.

The problem raised by Tomohiro Fukaya around 2014 addresses exactly this point: are Γ∞\Gamma^\inftyΓ∞, Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/Z2​ and Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/U(1) pairwise non-similar? Two pyramids P,Q\mathcal P,\mathcal QP,Q are similar if aP=Qa\mathcal P=\mathcal QaP=Q for some a>0a>0a>0, where aPa\mathcal PaP is obtained by multiplying the distances of all members of P\mathcal PP by aaa. In other words, the question is whether the effect of forgetting sign or phase can be absorbed by a change of the unit of distance. The paper resolves it affirmatively (Theorem A, stated in the Result section).

How much of a difference visible in finite dimensions survives in the limit? The paper's strategy has three steps.

  1. Separating the Gaussian from the quotients. Compute the sharp constant C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ controlling the fluctuation of observables for the three pyramids: it is 111 for the Gaussian and 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ for both quotients (Theorem B). Then use the separation coefficient ΘPI\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}ΘPI​, which does not depend on the unit of distance: it is 222 for the Gaussian and 444 for both quotients (Theorem C).
  2. Agreement of the two quotients. These two numbers agree exactly for Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/Z2​ and Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/U(1), so a different invariant is needed.
  3. Strictness of an inclusion. The phase quotient is contained in the sign quotient. A half-line carrying the half-normal distribution does not belong to the former, and this is shown by a constraint on third moments (Theorem D).

The plan of the page: first define the objects, then prepare the pyramid and two invariants as the language for limits, then state the results together and follow the proofs step by step.

Object | The sign and phase quotients are built by applying one transformation to all coordinates at once

Fix the finite-dimensional models to be compared. The standard normal distribution N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) is the probability distribution on the real line with density (2π)−1/2e−t2/2(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}(2π)−1/2e−t2/2. Γn=(Rn,∥⋅∥2,γn). \Gamma^n=(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|_2,\gamma^n). Γn=(Rn,∥⋅∥2​,γn).

Explainer's note. Let me compute the smallest case first. For a single real number the orbit is {x,−x}\{x,-x\}{x,−x}, and matching [x][x][x] with ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ identifies the quotient with a half-line. The distance is

min⁡{∣x−y∣,∣x+y∣}=∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣, \min\{|x-y|,|x+y|\}=\bigl||x|-|y|\bigr|, min{∣x−y∣,∣x+y∣}=​∣x∣−∣y∣​,

inf⁡θ∣z−eiθw∣=∣∣z∣−∣w∣∣. \inf_\theta|z-e^{i\theta}w|=\bigl||z|-|w|\bigr|. θinf​∣z−eiθw∣=​∣z∣−∣w∣​.

The two distributions on the half-line came from one observation, the radius. In general, to study observations on a quotient space it is convenient to study them on the original Gaussian space. The next lemma provides that bridge. Here a 111-Lipschitz function is a function whose values differ by at most the distance of the points.

Lemma 2.1 (claim of v2). Let a compact group GGG act on an mm-space XXX by measure-preserving isometries. The quotient map πG:X→X/G\pi_G:X\to X/GπG​:X→X/G is a measure-preserving 111-Lipschitz map. Conversely, a GGG-invariant f∈Lip1(X)f\in\mathrm{Lip}_1(X)f∈Lip1​(X) determines a unique fˉ:X/G→R\bar f:X/G\to\mathbb Rfˉ​:X/G→R with f=fˉ∘πGf=\bar f\circ\pi_Gf=fˉ​∘πG​, and this fˉ\bar ffˉ​ is also 111-Lipschitz. If GGG acts on two spaces and a measure-preserving 111-Lipschitz map TTT satisfies T(gx)=gT(x)T(gx)=gT(x)T(gx)=gT(x), then Tˉ([x])=[T(x)]\bar T([x])=[T(x)]Tˉ([x])=[T(x)] is a measure-preserving 111-Lipschitz map.

The converse direction is short to check. For an invariant fff put fˉ([x])=f(x)\bar f([x])=f(x)fˉ​([x])=f(x); the value does not depend on the representative. For any g∈Gg\in Gg∈G,

∣fˉ([x])−fˉ([y])∣=∣f(x)−f(gy)∣≤dX(x,gy), |\bar f([x])-\bar f([y])|=|f(x)-f(gy)|\leq d_X(x,gy), ∣fˉ​([x])−fˉ​([y])∣=∣f(x)−f(gy)∣≤dX​(x,gy),

and taking the infimum of the right-hand side over ggg gives 111-Lipschitz continuity for the quotient distance. The geometry of the quotient space can therefore be studied as the geometry of invariant Gaussian observations.

Tool | A limit of spaces is expressed by a pyramid collecting their observations

As the dimension increases, the Gaussian space becomes a different space each time. Points cannot be stacked and a limit taken pointwise, so we collect all the observations that can be extracted from each space and compare the limits of these collections. As the preceding lemma showed, observations on a quotient are exactly invariant observations. This section prepares the pyramid, a collection of observations, and the definitions of the three limits.

A space equipped with a distance and a probability is called an mm-space. Precisely, it is a pair of a complete separable metric space XXX and a Borel probability measure μX\mu_XμX​ on it. Complete means that Cauchy sequences have limits in the space; separable means that countably many points approximate the whole space to any precision. We consider measures whose support (the set of points every neighborhood of which has positive probability) is the whole space. Two mm-spaces are identified if there is a measure-preserving isometry between their supports (Definition 1.1).

When f:Y→Xf:Y\to Xf:Y→X does not increase distances, that is,

dX(f(y),f(y′))≤dY(y,y′), d_X(f(y),f(y'))\leq d_Y(y,y'), dX​(f(y),f(y′))≤dY​(y,y′),

and moreover f∗μY=μXf_*\mu_Y=\mu_Xf∗​μY​=μX​, we write X≺YX\prec YX≺Y (Definition 1.3). This says that the distance and probability of XXX can be extracted from YYY without amplifying distances. For example, the map taking the first coordinate of Γn\Gamma^nΓn gives Γ1≺Γn\Gamma^1\prec\Gamma^nΓ1≺Γn. The map need not be bijective: even if many points collapse to the same observed value, the distribution of observed values and the distances among them remain. A real-valued function that does not increase distance is called below a 111-Lipschitz observation.

Collect all mm-spaces obtainable from a space YYY as PY={X:X≺Y}\mathcal P_Y=\{X:X\prec Y\}PY​={X:X≺Y}. A generalization of such a collection is a pyramid.

Definition 1.4 (v2). A pyramid is a nonempty family P\mathcal PP of isomorphism classes of mm-spaces satisfying three conditions. (i) If X∈PX\in\mathcal PX∈P and Y≺XY\prec XY≺X, then Y∈PY\in\mathcal PY∈P. (ii) For any X,Y∈PX,Y\in\mathcal PX,Y∈P there is Z∈PZ\in\mathcal PZ∈P with X≺ZX\prec ZX≺Z and Y≺ZY\prec ZY≺Z. (iii) P\mathcal PP is closed with respect to the box distance.

The box distance describes the choices of points from two spaces by common random variables, and measures whether distances become uniformly close for most pairs of points. Condition (iii) is the operation of "including the limits", and it matters in later proofs. Definitions 1.1–1.4

Definition of the box distance

Give I=[0,1)I=[0,1)I=[0,1) the Lebesgue probability measure L1\mathcal L^1L1. Let φ:I→X\varphi:I\to Xφ:I→X and ψ:I→Y\psi:I\to Yψ:I→Y be Borel maps realizing the probabilities of the two spaces, that is, φ∗L1=μX\varphi_*\mathcal L^1=\mu_Xφ∗​L1=μX​ and ψ∗L1=μY\psi_*\mathcal L^1=\mu_Yψ∗​L1=μY​. The box distance □(X,Y)\Box(X,Y)□(X,Y) is the infimum of those ε≥0\varepsilon\geq0ε≥0 for which some Borel set I0⊂II_0\subset II0​⊂I satisfies L1(I0)≥1−ε\mathcal L^1(I_0)\geq1-\varepsilonL1(I0​)≥1−ε and

∣dX(φ(s),φ(t))−dY(ψ(s),ψ(t))∣≤ε(s,t∈I0). \left|d_X(\varphi(s),\varphi(t))-d_Y(\psi(s),\psi(t))\right| \leq\varepsilon\qquad(s,t\in I_0). ∣dX​(φ(s),φ(t))−dY​(ψ(s),ψ(t))∣≤ε(s,t∈I0​).

Definition 1.2

The limit of a sequence of pyramids is defined by weak convergence. For an mm-space XXX and a pyramid P\mathcal PP put □(X,P)=inf⁡Y∈P□(X,Y)\Box(X,\mathcal P)=\inf_{Y\in\mathcal P}\Box(X,Y)□(X,P)=infY∈P​□(X,Y). A sequence Pn\mathcal P_nPn​ converges weakly to P\mathcal PP if □(X,Pn)→0\Box(X,\mathcal P_n)\to0□(X,Pn​)→0 for every X∈PX\in\mathcal PX∈P, and lim inf⁡n□(X,Pn)>0\liminf_n\Box(X,\mathcal P_n)>0liminfn​□(X,Pn​)>0 for every X∉PX\notin\mathcal PX∈/P (Definition 1.5). A space in the limit can be approximated, and a space outside the limit stays at positive distance.

The projection that discards one coordinate is a measure-preserving 111-Lipschitz map commuting with the actions of Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ and U(1)U(1)U(1). By Lemma 2.1 this gives the chains

Γn≺Γn+1,Γn/Z2≺Γn+1/Z2,ΓCn/U(1)≺ΓCn+1/U(1). \Gamma^n\prec\Gamma^{n+1},\qquad \Gamma^n/\mathbb Z_2\prec\Gamma^{n+1}/\mathbb Z_2,\qquad \Gamma^n_{\mathbb C}/U(1)\prec\Gamma^{n+1}_{\mathbb C}/U(1). Γn≺Γn+1,Γn/Z2​≺Γn+1/Z2​,ΓCn​/U(1)≺ΓCn+1​/U(1).

The corresponding PY\mathcal P_YPY​ increase with the dimension. The box closures of their unions define the three pyramids.

Γ∞=⋃n≥1PΓn‾,Γ∞/Z2=⋃n≥1PΓn/Z2‾,Γ∞/U(1)=⋃n≥1PΓCn/U(1)‾. \begin{aligned} \Gamma^\infty &=\overline{\bigcup_{n\geq1}\mathcal P_{\Gamma^n}},\\ \Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2 &=\overline{\bigcup_{n\geq1}\mathcal P_{\Gamma^n/\mathbb Z_2}},\\ \Gamma^\infty/U(1) &=\overline{\bigcup_{n\geq1}\mathcal P_{\Gamma^n_{\mathbb C}/U(1)}}. \end{aligned} Γ∞Γ∞/Z2​Γ∞/U(1)​=n≥1⋃​PΓn​​,=n≥1⋃​PΓn/Z2​​​,=n≥1⋃​PΓCn​/U(1)​​.​

The paper states in §1.2 that these three increasing sequences converge weakly to the respective limits in the sense above, and uses this as a property from pyramid theory. This is not convergence on a common set of points. With this definition, an infinite family of independent normal variables never has to be treated as one point of an ordinary Euclidean space; the objects compared are families of mm-spaces. §1.2

Explainer's note. The meaning of taking the closure deserves attention. That XXX belongs to the sign-quotient family includes not only the case where XXX can be extracted directly from a finite-dimensional sign quotient, but also the case where extractable spaces approach XXX in the box distance. The fact that a space "lies in no finite dimension" therefore does not prove that it is outside the limit. This is why estimates independent of the dimension become necessary later.

Multiplication of distances by a>0a>0a>0 is written aXaXaX for an mm-space and aP={aX:X∈P}a\mathcal P=\{aX:X\in\mathcal P\}aP={aX:X∈P} for a pyramid. Two pyramids are similar if aP=Qa\mathcal P=\mathcal QaP=Q for some a>0a>0a>0.

Tool | The size of fluctuation and the remoteness of tails can be turned into ratios independent of the unit of distance

A pyramid is a family of spaces, so it cannot be examined by points or coordinates. We need numbers defined for the whole family. The paper uses two: first, a sharp constant bounding the variance of observations by the size of their variation; second, a separation distance measuring how far a set of large probability can be pulled from a set of small probability.

Poincaré constant. The (2,2)(2,2)(2,2)-Poincaré constant C2,2(X)C_{2,2}(X)C2,2​(X) of an mm-space XXX is the infimum of the nonnegative constants CCC such that

Var⁡μX(f)≤C2∫Xlip⁡a(f)2 dμX \operatorname{Var}_{\mu_X}(f)\leq C^2\int_X\operatorname{lip}_{\mathrm a}(f)^2\,d\mu_X VarμX​​(f)≤C2∫X​lipa​(f)2dμX​

holds for every bounded Lipschitz function f:X→Rf:X\to\mathbb Rf:X→R (Definition 1.6). Here Var⁡μX(f)=∫X(f−∫Xf dμX)2 dμX\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_X}(f)=\int_X(f-\int_Xf\,d\mu_X)^2\,d\mu_XVarμX​​(f)=∫X​(f−∫X​fdμX​)2dμX​, and lip⁡a(f)(x)\operatorname{lip}_{\mathrm a}(f)(x)lipa​(f)(x) is the limit as r↓0r\downarrow0r↓0 of the Lipschitz constant of fff on the ball of radius rrr around xxx (the asymptotic Lipschitz constant). For a smooth function on Euclidean space it corresponds to the length ∥∇f(x)∥2\|\nabla f(x)\|_2∥∇f(x)∥2​ of the gradient. A space with smaller CCC can produce less variance from the same amount of variation. For a pyramid take the supremum over its members, C2,2(P)=sup⁡X∈PC2,2(X)C_{2,2}(\mathcal P)=\sup_{X\in\mathcal P}C_{2,2}(X)C2,2​(P)=supX∈P​C2,2​(X), the standard extension of Esaki–Kazukawa–Mitsuishi [2].

Separation distance. For 0<α,β≤10<\alpha,\beta\leq10<α,β≤1, Sep⁡(X;α,β)\operatorname{Sep}(X;\alpha,\beta)Sep(X;α,β) is the supremum of the set distance dX(A,B)=inf⁡x∈A,y∈BdX(x,y)d_X(A,B)=\inf_{x\in A,y\in B}d_X(x,y)dX​(A,B)=infx∈A,y∈B​dX​(x,y) over Borel sets A,BA,BA,B of probability at least α,β\alpha,\betaα,β respectively (Definition 1.7). Sep⁡(P;α,β)=lim⁡δ↓0sup⁡X∈PSep⁡(X;α−δ,β−δ) \operatorname{Sep}(\mathcal P;\alpha,\beta) =\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\sup_{X\in\mathcal P} \operatorname{Sep}(X;\alpha-\delta,\beta-\delta) Sep(P;α,β)=δ↓0lim​X∈Psup​Sep(X;α−δ,β−δ)

(Definition 1.8, 0<δ<min⁡{α,β}0<\delta<\min\{\alpha,\beta\}0<δ<min{α,β}): the probability conditions are loosened slightly before the limit is taken. Definitions 1.6–1.8

Multiplying distances by aaa multiplies both C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ and Sep⁡\operatorname{Sep}Sep by aaa. So for 0<C2,2(P)<∞0<C_{2,2}(\mathcal P)<\infty0<C2,2​(P)<∞ we consider the ratio in which the unit of distance cancels,

ΘPI(P)=lim sup⁡κ↓0Sep⁡(P;1/2,κ)2C2,2(P)2log⁡(1/κ). \Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}(\mathcal P) =\limsup_{\kappa\downarrow0} \frac{\operatorname{Sep}(\mathcal P;1/2,\kappa)^2} {C_{2,2}(\mathcal P)^2\log(1/\kappa)}. ΘPI​(P)=κ↓0limsup​C2,2​(P)2log(1/κ)Sep(P;1/2,κ)2​.

Since ΘPI(aP)=ΘPI(P)\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}(a\mathcal P)=\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}(\mathcal P)ΘPI​(aP)=ΘPI​(P), the value does not change under similarity. Hence if ΘPI\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}ΘPI​ differs, the two pyramids are not similar. If only C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ differs, on the other hand, the values can be matched by enlarging or shrinking distances. This is why ΘPI\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}ΘPI​ is examined after C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​.

Result | Two invariants and an inclusion distinguish the three pyramids

Compute the two numbers prepared in the previous section for the three pyramids. The paper's claims are the following four.

Proof | C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ equals 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ by the spectral gap of even functions (Theorem B)

The first difference in the table is 111 for the Gaussian against 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ for the quotients. In this section we squeeze 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ from above and below, using that an observation on a quotient is invariant and in particular an even function.

Explainer's note. Here is the overall idea first. A function on Gaussian space splits into components by the degree of Hermite polynomials. The higher the degree of a component, the more gradient energy is needed to produce the same amount of variation, and the cheapest way to produce variation is the first-degree component. An observation that forgets sign (an even function) has no first-degree component, so the cheapest way rises to degree two. The variance obtainable from the same energy becomes smaller, and the constant drops from 111 to 1/21/\sqrt21/2​.

Pulling an observation on a quotient back by the quotient map gives an even function for the quotient by Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ and a function invariant under phase rotation for the quotient by U(1)U(1)U(1). The latter is also even because −1∈U(1)-1\in U(1)−1∈U(1). Conversely, an invariant 111-Lipschitz function is a 111-Lipschitz function on the quotient (Lemma 2.1).

We prepare the tools of Gaussian analysis. Write ⟨u,v⟩=∫uv dγn\langle u,v\rangle=\int uv\,d\gamma^n⟨u,v⟩=∫uvdγn for the inner product of functions and ∥u∥p=(∫∣u∣p dγn)1/p\|u\|_p=(\int|u|^p\,d\gamma^n)^{1/p}∥u∥p​=(∫∣u∣pdγn)1/p for the LpL^pLp norm. Explainer's note. Let me state the paper's strategy (from the introduction) in advance. If H1H_1H1​ belonged to the phase-quotient pyramid, we would obtain a sequence of phase-invariant 111-Lipschitz observations rjr_jrj​ whose distributions approach the half-normal distribution. But phase invariance imposes an upper bound on the third moment of a quadratic form, and the value coming from the half-normal distribution exceeds it. The four steps of the next section verify this route one step at a time.

We carry out the route described in the previous section as the proof of Theorem 5.5 in four steps. Step 1 replaces the membership assumption by a sequence of observations, step 2 brings their squares close to quadratic forms, step 3 shows an upper bound for the third moment of phase-invariant quadratic forms, and step 4 extracts the clash between that bound and the limiting value.

A phase rotation z↦eiθzz\mapsto e^{i\theta}zz↦eiθz is an orthogonal transformation of R2Nj\mathbb R^{2N_j}R2Nj​, so if hjh_jhj​ is invariant under it, so is qj=P2hjq_j=P_2h_jqj​=P2​hj​. Strictly speaking, the equality obtained from the projection holds almost everywhere; but qjq_jqj​ is a continuous polynomial and the Gaussian measure gives positive probability to every open ball, so the equality holds at every point.

Phase-invariant quadratic forms have an upper bound on the third moment.

Lemma 5.4 (claim of v2). If a quadratic form q∈Q2Nq\in\mathcal Q_{2N}q∈Q2N​ on CN≃R2N\mathbb C^N\simeq\mathbb R^{2N}CN≃R2N is phase-invariant, there are complex orthonormal coordinates z=(z1,…,zN)z=(z_1,\dots,z_N)z=(z1​,…,zN​) and real numbers λ1,…,λN\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_Nλ1​,…,λN​ with q(z)=∑k=1Nλk(∣zk∣2−2),q(z)=\sum_{k=1}^N\lambda_k(|z_k|^2-2),q(z)=k=1∑N​λk​(∣zk​∣2−2),

∫q2 dγ2N=4∑kλk2,∫q3 dγ2N=16∑kλk3,\int q^2\,d\gamma^{2N}=4\sum_k\lambda_k^2,\qquad\int q^3\,d\gamma^{2N}=16\sum_k\lambda_k^3,∫q2dγ2N=4k∑​λk2​,∫q3dγ2N=16k∑​λk3​,

and hence the third moment is at most 2(∫q2 dγ2N)3/22(\int q^2\,d\gamma^{2N})^{3/2}2(∫q2dγ2N)3/2.

Distinction from the source. The source states Lemma 5.4 as the upper bound ∫q3≤2(∫q2)3/2\int q^3\leq2(\int q^2)^{3/2}∫q3≤2(∫q2)3/2 without absolute value, while the proof of Theorem 5.5 uses the form with absolute value, ∣Eqj3∣≤2(Eqj2)3/2|\mathbb Eq_j^3|\leq2(\mathbb Eq_j^2)^{3/2}∣Eqj3​∣≤2(Eqj2​)3/2. Since −q-q−q is also a phase-invariant quadratic form, the form with absolute value follows from the same lemma. This page states it with the absolute value. Step 4 uses only the upper estimate of Eqj3\mathbb Eq_j^3Eqj3​, so the difference in notation does not affect the argument (as far as I re-read it for this page).

The key of the proof is linear algebra. Phase invariance forces the real symmetric matrix AAA representing the quadratic form to commute with the complex structure JJJ (the map corresponding to "multiplication by iii"), AJ=JAAJ=JAAJ=JA. Then AAA is complex linear and Hermitian with respect to the complex inner product, and can be diagonalized in a complex orthonormal basis. As a real matrix it has the form diag⁡(λ1I2,…,λNI2)\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1I_2,\dots,\lambda_NI_2)diag(λ1​I2​,…,λN​I2​), each λk\lambda_kλk​ appearing once for the real part and once for the imaginary part.

Why phase invariance pairs two real coordinates with the same coefficient

Write q(x)=xTAx−tr⁡Aq(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax-\operatorname{tr}Aq(x)=xTAx−trA and J(xk,yk)=(−yk,xk)J(x_k,y_k)=(-y_k,x_k)J(xk​,yk​)=(−yk​,xk​). The phase rotation UθU_\thetaUθ​ equals eθJe^{\theta J}eθJ, and JT=−JJ^{\mathsf T}=-JJT=−J. Since q(Uθx)=q(x)q(U_\theta x)=q(x)q(Uθ​x)=q(x) holds at every point, uniqueness of the symmetric-matrix representation of a quadratic form gives UθTAUθ=AU_\theta^{\mathsf T}AU_\theta=AUθT​AUθ​=A. Differentiating at θ=0\theta=0θ=0 gives −JA+AJ=0-JA+AJ=0−JA+AJ=0, that is, A(iw)=iA(w)A(iw)=iA(w)A(iw)=iA(w), so AAA is also complex linear. Real symmetry means symmetry with respect to the real part of the complex inner product; replacing one argument by iwiwiw gives the same equality for the imaginary part, so AAA is Hermitian with respect to the complex inner product. A Hermitian matrix can be diagonalized in a complex orthonormal basis (with real eigenvalues). This change of coordinates preserves the real Euclidean distance, so the transformed real and imaginary parts are again independent standard normal variables. Then xTAx=∑kλk∣zk∣2x^{\mathsf T}Ax=\sum_k\lambda_k|z_k|^2xTAx=∑k​λk​∣zk​∣2 and tr⁡A=2∑kλk\operatorname{tr}A=2\sum_k\lambda_ktrA=2∑k​λk​, which gives the stated expression.

For sign reversal alone every quadratic form is even, so no additional condition like AJ=JAAJ=JAAJ=JA arises. This condition, needed only when the common phase is forgotten, is what separates the two quotients.

The moments can be computed directly. For independent standard normal variables ξk,ηk\xi_k,\eta_kξk​,ηk​ put Wk=ξk2+ηk2−2=(ξk2−1)+(ηk2−1)W_k=\xi_k^2+\eta_k^2-2=(\xi_k^2-1)+(\eta_k^2-1)Wk​=ξk2​+ηk2​−2=(ξk2​−1)+(ηk2​−1). Each bracket has mean 000, second moment 222 and third moment 888. By independence and mean zero the mixed terms vanish, so

EWk=0,EWk2=2+2=4,EWk3=8+8=16. \mathbb EW_k=0,\qquad\mathbb EW_k^2=2+2=4,\qquad\mathbb EW_k^3=8+8=16 . EWk​=0,EWk2​=2+2=4,EWk3​=8+8=16.

so ∣Eq3∣≤16(∑kλk2)3/2=2(Eq2)3/2|\mathbb Eq^3|\leq16(\sum_k\lambda_k^2)^{3/2}=2(\mathbb Eq^2)^{3/2}∣Eq3∣≤16(∑k​λk2​)3/2=2(Eq2)3/2. The constant 222 does not change when the dimension or the number of eigenvalues grows, so it applies to the sequence qjq_jqj​.

Explainer's note. Comparing with the real case shows what this constant means. Diagonalizing a real symmetric matrix AAA by an orthogonal transformation, a real quadratic form can be written q=∑iλi(ξi2−1)q=\sum_i\lambda_i(\xi_i^2-1)q=∑i​λi​(ξi2​−1). Then Eq2=2∑λi2\mathbb Eq^2=2\sum\lambda_i^2Eq2=2∑λi2​ and Eq3=8∑λi3\mathbb Eq^3=8\sum\lambda_i^3Eq3=8∑λi3​, so the constant of the same argument is 8/23/2=228/2^{3/2}=2\sqrt28/23/2=22​, and the one-coordinate form q=ξ2−1q=\xi^2-1q=ξ2−1 (Eq2=2\mathbb Eq^2=2Eq2=2, Eq3=8\mathbb Eq^3=8Eq3=8) attains equality. In the sign quotient, the values (2,8)(2,8)(2,8) produced by the half-normal distribution are exactly allowed. In the phase quotient, the real and imaginary parts form a pair with the same coefficient, which lowers the constant from 222\sqrt222​ to 222, and (2,8)(2,8)(2,8) is not allowed.

8≤2⋅23/2=42, 8\leq2\cdot2^{3/2}=4\sqrt2 , 8≤2⋅23/2=42​,

but 42≈5.66<84\sqrt2\approx5.66<842​≈5.66<8, a contradiction. Therefore H1∉Γ∞/U(1)H_1\notin\Gamma^\infty/U(1)H1​∈/Γ∞/U(1), and the inclusion (5.1) is strict.

Theorem D (proof completed). By Theorem 5.5 and the inclusion (5.1), Γ∞/U(1)⊊Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/U(1)\subsetneq\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/U(1)⊊Γ∞/Z2​.

Consequence | Pairwise non-similarity of the three follows from two comparisons

The three comparisons are now in place. The non-similarity of the Gaussian and each quotient was already obtained in Corollary 4.6. The two quotients are handled by the following Corollary 5.6.

Corollary 5.6 (claim of v2). For any b,c>0b,c>0b,c>0, b(Γ∞/Z2)≠c(Γ∞/U(1))b(\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2)\neq c(\Gamma^\infty/U(1))b(Γ∞/Z2​)=c(Γ∞/U(1)).

The proof is short. If they were equal, Theorem B and the homogeneity of degree 111 of C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ would give

b2=C2,2(b(Γ∞/Z2))=C2,2(c(Γ∞/U(1)))=c2, \frac b{\sqrt2}=C_{2,2}(b(\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2))=C_{2,2}(c(\Gamma^\infty/U(1)))=\frac c{\sqrt2}, 2​b​=C2,2​(b(Γ∞/Z2​))=C2,2​(c(Γ∞/U(1)))=2​c​,

so b=cb=cb=c. Multiplying both sides by 1/b1/b1/b would give Γ∞/Z2=Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2=\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/Z2​=Γ∞/U(1), contradicting Theorem 5.5.

The proof of Theorem A just combines Corollary 4.6 (the Gaussian is similar to neither quotient) and Corollary 5.6 (the two quotients are not similar). Hence no two of the three pyramids are similar.

For the two quotients, both the sharp constant controlling fluctuations and the separation coefficient of the far tail coincide. Still, the families of mm-spaces they contain differ. To capture this difference, the paper turned membership in the limit back into approximation of observations, passed through approximation by quadratic forms, and used the third-moment constraint imposed by phase symmetry.

Limits | What relies on external theorems, and what this page does not cover

The Consequence section completed the pairwise non-similarity. Here we sort out what its proof depends on and how far the claim reaches. The proofs on this page take the following known results as input; their proofs are left to the sources and they are stated in usable form: the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality (Borell [1], Sudakov–Tsirel'son [19]); completeness of Hermite polynomials and the energy identity (Nualart [8]); the hypercontractive estimate for quadratic forms (Nelson [13], Nualart [8]); the Sobolev chain rule for Lipschitz functions (Evans–Gariepy [3]); the Mills-ratio estimate of the normal tail (Gordon [9]); the transfer of C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ to pyramids and the Gaussian value C2,2(Γ∞)=1C_{2,2}(\Gamma^\infty)=1C2,2​(Γ∞)=1 (Esaki–Kazukawa–Mitsuishi [2]); the limit formula for the separation distance (Ozawa–Shioya [14]); the theory of box convergence and pyramids together with the weak convergence of the increasing sequences stated in §1.2 (Shioya [15, 16], Gromov [10]).

The reach of the claim is also limited. Theorem D shows strictness of the inclusion by a single witness, the half-line H1H_1H1​ with the half-normal distribution. It does not describe all spaces that belong to Γ∞/Z2\Gamma^\infty/\mathbb Z_2Γ∞/Z2​ but not to Γ∞/U(1)\Gamma^\infty/U(1)Γ∞/U(1). The agreement of C2,2C_{2,2}C2,2​ and ΘPI\Theta_{\mathrm{PI}}ΘPI​ on the two quotients only shows that these two quantities do not separate them; the ground for separation came from the upper bound on the third moment. The paper itself says that the result suggests studying other Gaussian quotients through the interaction of invariant observations, their low-degree components and moment constraints.
